newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-GIRARDELLI TO ANNOUNCE RETIREMENT.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-GIRARDELLI TO ANNOUNCE RETIREMENT.

text.p: After winning more medals and titles than any other man and putting Luxembourg on the Alpine skiing map, time and injuries have caught up with Marc Girardelli.
The five times overall World Cup champion, who has not raced since December, will announce his retirement next week.

Sources close to the all-rounder, who has won a record 13 medals from six world championships and three Olympics in a 17-year career, say that he will hold a news conference on Monday to declare the end.
The 33-year-old Austrian-born skier, who had been due to defend his 1996 combined title at the world championships in Italy this week, has not turned up in Sestriere.
He has said nothing but the word is out that his career of 46 World Cup wins and four gold medals is over.
If true, and nobody in skiing doubts it, there would be a painful irony in the choice of location.
It was here in 1986 that he dislocated a shoulder after crashing in a slalom. Despite the pain, he won his first gold medals two months later in Crans Montana.
Then, in a World Cup super-giant slalom in Sestriere in 1989, the reigning overall champion suffered a crash that almost killed him from internal bleeding discovered later.
The Italian daily sports newspaper Tuttosport said in a headline on Tuesday: "Girardelli, it's really over."
The paper, which has good contacts with Girardelli's main sponsors, said doctors had barred the skier from racing the men's combined and he would call it a day.
Those who have followed Girardelli's progress this season in his handful of races could not be surprised.
He struggled in the opening giant slalom in Soelden, Austria, and said that just qualifying was a success.
The sporting obituaries have been prepared since he finished 57th in the first of two downhills held in Val Gardena before Christmas. There were only 60 racers on the hill.
"I am simply exhausted. I have no more energy after each run. I just cannot make it," he said at the time.
Girardelli, showing flashes of his former self, had set the best intermediate time at the start of that race but was physically shattered long before the finish.
He went to see specialists in Munich afterwards, who diagnosed that he had damaged the only ligaments in his knees that had previously been unscathed in his career.

Before the season started, he had suffered back and kidney problems following his crash in the giant slalom at Sierra Nevada and went to health spas in Slovenia and elsewhere in Europe in a desperate search for a cure.
Injury has scarred Girardelli like few other Alpine skiers and even friends say that he now has the body of an old man after 13 major operations spanning two decades.
"I should become a surgeon because I know perfectly each muscle and joint in the human body," he once said.
As a boy Girardelli trained and competed with a regional team in Vorarlberg, in eastern Austria.
When he was selected to go to a special school for young racers, his father Helmut -- who had his own ideas on his son's future as an athlete -- decided otherwise.
The resulting clash with the regional Austrian ski powers led to Girardelli turning his back on his country.

When he was 14, the Girardelli family looked about for another country and reached an agreement with the Luxembourg ski federation which gave him an international licence which allowed him to take part in international events at 16.
There was no family connection with the tiny, and above all flat, European nation but that did not matter.
Two years later, Girardelli made his World Cup debut. He had his first podium the next year, finishing second in a slalom at Wengen ahead of his Swedish hero Ingemar Stenmark.
He won his first race in March 1983 in Gallivare, Sweden.
A few weeks later he had his first big accident, at Lake Louise in Canada where he tore left knee ligaments.
"I was afraid Marc would not be able to ski again," said doctor Richard Steadma at the time.
"To race again seemed at that point totally impossible. He is the most extraordinary athlete I have ever met."
